slides.title: Symmetric Spaces
slides.notes: Open by presenting the chapter as the point where geodesic symmetry becomes an organizing principle rather than a local trick. The audience should hear three strands immediately: affine connections, homogeneous spaces, and Lie algebra splittings. The deck will keep those strands visible on every slide.

slides.title: Chapter Route
slides.notes: Use this map to prevent the lecture from feeling like a list of definitions. The chapter first extracts symmetry from affine geometry, then encodes it in a group and Lie algebra, then specializes to Riemannian and Hermitian settings where curvature, duality, examples, and classification become concrete.

slides.title: Local Symmetry At A Point
slides.notes: Emphasize that the first object is local and geometric. In normal coordinates, the symmetry at a point reverses tangent vectors through the exponential map. This is not yet a group action on the whole manifold; it is a test for whether the affine connection looks identical in opposite geodesic directions.

slides.title: The Affine Criterion
slides.notes: Explain the criterion as a compression of many coordinate identities into two invariant statements. Torsion must vanish because a point reflection reverses odd first-order asymmetry. Curvature must be parallel because the same curvature model is seen after moving by affine symmetries from point to point.

slides.title: From Symmetries To A Triple
slides.notes: The homogeneous triple is the chapter's first major translation. Choose a base point, collect connected affine transformations, record the isotropy subgroup, and let the base-point symmetry conjugate the transformation group. The fixed subgroup condition says that isotropy is exactly the group-level shadow of reflection.

slides.title: The Lie Algebra Split
slides.notes: Pause on the eigenspace decomposition because it drives nearly every later formula. The plus part is infinitesimal isotropy and the minus part identifies with tangent vectors at the base point. The bracket table is the algebraic replacement for geometric reflection rules.

slides.title: Canonical Connection
slides.notes: The canonical connection is the reverse construction: start from the symmetric triple and recover an affine symmetric geometry on the quotient. At the origin, the connection is as simple as possible on the tangent part, while curvature is still present through the isotropy bracket.

slides.title: Riemannian Symmetric Spaces
slides.notes: Specialize carefully. A Riemannian symmetric space is not just a symmetric space with a metric attached; its geodesic symmetries are isometries and the canonical connection becomes Levi-Civita. Completeness and transitivity make local reflection data into global geometry.

slides.title: Totally Geodesic Submanifolds
slides.notes: This slide is the main bridge from global space to subspace testing. A submanifold is totally geodesic when geodesics that start tangent remain inside. In the symmetric algebra, that geometric condition becomes a triple bracket closure, which is much easier to check in examples.

slides.title: Structure Of Symmetric Lie Algebras
slides.notes: Frame this as algebraic bookkeeping with geometric consequences. Radical and semisimple pieces must respect the involution, and direct-sum decompositions of symmetric Lie algebras mirror product decompositions of spaces. The point is not classification yet, but a controlled reduction of complexity.

slides.title: Irreducible Factors
slides.notes: Connect the algebraic reductions to de Rham decomposition. A simply connected Riemannian symmetric space splits into Euclidean and irreducible factors, and each factor is again symmetric. Classification can therefore focus on irreducible orthogonal symmetric Lie algebras rather than arbitrary products.

slides.title: Compact And Noncompact Types
slides.notes: The Killing form supplies a sign test for the two major Riemannian families. Compact type has curvature with nonnegative behavior and compact models, while noncompact type has the dual sign and often Euclidean-like topology. Stress that the same bracket data is being read with different metric signs.

slides.title: Duality
slides.notes: Duality is the chapter's elegant mechanism for pairing examples. The isotropy algebra is kept fixed while tangent directions are multiplied by an imaginary unit at the algebraic level. In geometric terms, this flips the curvature sign and pairs compact spaces with noncompact companions.

slides.title: Sphere And Hyperbolic Models
slides.notes: Use the two rank-one models as an anchor before introducing larger families. Both are quotients by the same isotropy type, and both have large symmetry groups. Their geodesic subspaces show why the bracket closure test is not abstract: it literally selects lower-dimensional copies inside the model.

slides.title: Grassmann And Projective Families
slides.notes: The examples section broadens the catalog from rank-one spaces to matrix quotients. Oriented Grassmannians, complex projective spaces, quadrics, and complex Grassmannians all carry the same pattern: a block matrix decomposition, an invariant metric, and symmetric subspaces detected algebraically.

slides.title: Hermitian Symmetric Spaces
slides.notes: Make the complex structure feel structural rather than decorative. In the Hermitian case, the tangent representation admits an invariant complex operator, often coming from a central isotropy element. The symmetries preserve both the metric and complex structure, so the geometry is automatically Kahler.

slides.title: Classification Outline
slides.notes: The final section is an outline, so present it as a pipeline rather than a table to memorize. Reduce to simply connected irreducible spaces, pass to orthogonal symmetric Lie algebras, use duality to focus on noncompact type, and then invoke the classification of real simple Lie algebras.

slides.title: Notebook Lab And Recap
slides.notes: Close by tying the lecture back to the notebook. The notebook's dependency graph, local curvature proxy, and symbolic invariant checks are small, but they model the correct reading habit. Students should leave able to test symmetry through geodesic reflections, bracket closure, curvature signs, and decomposition.
